title: A study testing a new pain treatment during heart surgery to help prevent long-term pain after heart bypass surgery
official: A randomised controlled trial to investigate the effectiveness of pectoralis-intercostal-rectus sheath plane block in reducing chronic post-sternotomy pain after cardiac surgery: to study feasibility for a substantive trial of nerve blOck in caRdIac surGery chronic paIN (ORIGIN-feasibility trial)
summary:
Background and study aims
Many people who have heart bypass surgery develop pain in their chest that lasts for months after the operation. This long-term pain can affect daily life, sleep, mood and recovery. Doctors currently use strong painkillers (opioids) to manage pain during and after surgery, but these can cause side effects such as sickness, drowsiness and breathing problems. This study is testing a new pain relief technique called a “nerve block,” given during and after surgery, to see if it might reduce long-term pain after heart bypass surgery. This study aims to find out whether it is possible to run a larger trial to fully test how effective this new technique is.

Who can participate?
Patients aged 16 years and over who are planning to have elective (planned) heart bypass surgery (CABG only) at NHS hospitals across the UK.

What does the study involve?
Participants will be assigned to one of two groups:
- New technique group: receives the nerve block during surgery
- Usual care group: receives standard pain treatment without the nerve block

Participants will:
- Complete questionnaires about pain, well-being and recovery before surgery and at set times afterwards, up to 6 months after their surgery.
- Have their pain levels recorded during their hospital stay
The study will also look at how easy it is to recruit participants, deliver the treatment and collect information for a future larger trial.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
Possible benefits:
The nerve block may improve pain control after surgery. Patients may need fewer strong pain medicines. Information from the study may help improve care for future patients undergoing heart surgery

Possible risks:
The nerve block involves injections, which carry small risks such as bleeding, infection, or nerve irritation.  Some questionnaires may include personal or sensitive questions, which some people might find uncomfortable. All treatments used in the study are already used in clinical practice, and participants will continue to receive standard care throughout.

Where is the study run from?
The study is coordinated by the Birmingham Clinical Trials Unit, University of Birmingham, UK.

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
Each participant will take part in the study for about 6 months after their surgery, with follow-up at 3 and 6 months.
The study is expected to start recruiting participants from July 2026 and will end by the end of January 2027.

Who is funding the study?
The National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) under its Research for Patient Benefit (RfPB) Programme, UK.

Who is the main contact?
Mary Nulty, Trial Manager: Origin@trials.bham.ac.uk

interventions.name:
This study will be a multi-centre, parallel, 2-arm, randomised controlled feasibility trial with 1:1 allocation of pectoralis-intercostal-rectus sheath plane(PIRS) block versus usual practice. 

The participants will be allocated to their group randomly using an online randomisation software embedde

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Aged 16 years old or over
2. Having elective coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) only
3. Able to provide informed consent
4. American Society of Anaesthesiologists physical status I, II or III
Exclusion criteria:
1. Contraindication to regional techniques, e.g., known allergy to local anaesthetics; infection near the proposed puncture site; severe coagulation disorders (in the clinician’s opinion)
2. Pregnancy
3. Surgery for combined coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) and valve surgery
4. Previous median sternotomy within 3 months
5. Likely inability to comply with completion of the study questionnaires
